2.30.m: The sages said: / That Vena whom you described as abiding in sinful conduct— / what was the livelihood of that sinful one, and what fruit did he obtain, O twice-born?
Relate the life of that Vena just as it was in ancient times / in detail to us, O best of knowers, O broad-minded one!
Sūta said: / I shall declare the life of that Vena, and also of the high-souled son of Vena— / which is very meritorious—properly, as it was heard of old.
When that son, the fortunate and high-souled Pṛthu, was born, / the king attained purity and once more attained righteousness.
All the great sins accumulated by the lowest of men / depart by contact with a sacred ford.
From the company of the virtuous, only merit arises, there is no doubt; / but from contact with the sinful, only sin arises.
Through conversation, sight, touch, sitting together, and dining, indeed, / and through the company of sinners, wrongdoing is transferred.
So too with the meritorious, merit alone is transferred. / By association with a great sacred ford, sinners are purified, not otherwise;
cleansed of all impurities, they go to an auspicious destination. / The sages said: / How then do those sinners attain the highest perfection, O best of twice-born?
Tell that to us at length; faith has arisen to hear it.
Sūta said: / Hunters and great sinners, having become servants and fishermen, / situated in the waters of the Revā, the Yamunā, and the Gaṅgā,
bathing knowingly or unknowingly and sporting in the water, / by contact with the great river attain the supreme destination.
Casting off their servitude and mass of sins, they go [to heaven]; / all of them are indeed bathed by contact with the holy water.
And by contact with the great river—not of others, O best of men— / even the sin of sinners among people of great merit is destroyed,
by contact, by sight, by touch; no hesitation should be made here. / Concerning this matter, O brahmins, a sin-destroying legendary history is heard;
that I will declare to you today, which bestows great merit. / There was a certain deer hunter named Sulobha in a great forest.
With dogs, net-snares, and bows and arrows, / he continually killed deer, lusting for the taste of meat.
Once that very wicked soul, bow in hand and holding an arrow, / surrounded by dogs, went to the impassable forest of the Vindhya.
He slew many frightened deer, antelopes, and wild boars. / Having reached the bank of the Revā, a certain killer of carp,
having slaughtered the carp, came out of the water. / Then a doe, terrified by fear of the deer-hunter Lobha,
devoted to saving her life, distressed, frightened, her mind bewildered, / running in haste, sought the bank of the Revā.
Chased by dogs, she was afflicted, wounded by the strike of an arrow. / Even with the speed of the wind, Sulabha, the killer of deer,
pursued right behind, while that doe ran in front. / The carp-killer saw her and stood ready, arrow in hand.
Bending his bow with speed, he obstructed that doe; / meanwhile, the hunter named Lobha arrived along with his dogs.
[Lobha said:] “She must not be slain; she is mine, she came into my hunt!” / Hearing his words, the fish-killer, lusting for meat,
the wicked-hearted, mighty one, released an arrow aimed at her. / Struck by the deer-hunter with a sharp arrow,
the doe died there by the arrows of the two wicked-minded men. / Attacked by the teeth of the dogs, she fell in haste
from the cliff into the sacred, sin-destroying pool of the Revā. / And those dogs, rushing forward, fell into the clear pool.
Fainting with anger, the deer-hunter said to the fisherman: / “This doe was mine, you villain! Why was she killed by your arrows?”
He, the fish-killer, spoke in turn to the deer-slayer: / “She is mine, there is no doubt! You speak with arrogance!”
Then the two of them fought each other; / out of anger and greed, those fortunate ones fell into the clear water.
At that time there was a great festival-day that grants liberation, / the conjunction of the new moon, which bestows the fruit of great merit.
All of them fell at the moment of that auspicious occasion, O best of men; / although devoid of prayer and meditation, and lacking devotion and truth,
by virtue of bathing in the sacred site, the doe, the dogs, and the hunter, / freed from all sins, went to the supreme destination.
By the power of sacred sites and through the company of the virtuous, O best of twice-born, / one destroys the sin of sinners as fire burns fuel.
Sūta said: / Thus by contact with those high-souled sages, / by conversation, sight, and touch, the king's
stain—the sin of Vena—was indeed destroyed of old through the company of the virtuous. / By contact with exceedingly fierce merit, the sin of sinners is destroyed;
by contact with exceedingly wicked sinners, sin alone is transferred. / By the fault of his maternal grandfather, that Vena was tainted.
The sages said: / What was the fault of his maternal grandfather? Tell us that in detail. / He is Death, he is Time, he is Yama and Dharma himself;
indeed, he is not violent to anyone, established in this post. / And the moving and unmoving worlds, abiding under the control of their own karma,
live, die, and experience [fruits] through their own actions. / Sinners behold him as terrible because of the ripening of their karma;
and in all the hells, one of great merit, by his karma, / would direct and strike, O Sūta—this Yama, day after day.
In all very meritorious deeds indeed, the righteous one engages him thus; no fault is seen in him.

[The sages said:] By what fault of Mṛtyu was the sinful Vena born?
Sūta said: Mṛtyu is the eternal punisher of the wicked-minded and sinful.

He acts in the form of Time and examines their deeds.
Whosoever has evil action, he causes him to be struck down by that very deed.

Knowing his sin, Yama thus leads him to what is beneficial;
[while] the well-doing soul attains heaven through his good deeds.

Mṛtyu himself joins all of them with good messengers,
with a great sense of happiness, making auspicious songs.

And he engages those who have made themselves [meritorious] with gifts, enjoyments, and the like,
and [the wicked] with diverse torments, afflictions, and harsh wooden [stocks].

Wrathful Mṛtyu frightens and strikes them, O brāhmaṇas;
thus indeed his activity revolves around their deeds.

And from Mṛtyu, O fortunate one, out of desire, from merit, was born
verily a daughter named Sunīthā to that great-souled one.

Considering her father's work while constantly playing,
she [observed him] as the punisher of creatures, watching over merit and sin.

That highly fortunate daughter of his, named Sunīthā,
while sporting, arrived at a forest surrounded by her female companions.

There she saw the highly fortunate, excellent son of a Gandharva,
named Suśaṅkha, son of Gītakolāhala, at that time.

She beheld him, beautiful in all his limbs, performing great austerity,
meditating on Sarasvatī for the sake of the complete attainment of the art of song.

She caused injury to him day after day.
Suśaṅkha constantly forgave [her] and said: "Go, go!"

Sent away, she would not go, and continued to cause obstacles.
Addressed by him, she became angry and struck him who was steadfast in austerity.

Then Suśaṅkha, enraged and overwhelmed by anger, said to her:
"O wicked one of sinful conduct, why has an obstacle been made by you?

Great persons do not return a blow because of being struck, O wicked one;
when cursed, they do not become angry—such is the firm rule of dharma.

By you I have been struck, O sinful one, [though] blameless and endowed with penance!"
Having spoken thus to Sunīthā who acted sinfully, that righteous one,

ceased from his great anger, knowing her to be a woman, and desisted.
Then she, whether out of sinful delusion or childishness, right here

said to that great-souled Suśaṅkha who was established in austerity:
"My father is the striker of the inhabitants of the three worlds.

He ever destroys the untrue and protects the true;
there is no fault in him, and he acts with great merit."

Having spoken thus, she went to her father and spoke these words:
"Father, by me was struck a son of a Gandharva in the forest,

performing penance always in solitude, free from lust and anger.
That righteous one, filled with anger and passion, said to me:

'One should never strike one who strikes, nor curse one who curses.'
Thus he spoke to me, father; tell me the reason for that!"

Thus addressed by Sunīthā, O best of the twice-born, that righteous Mṛtyu
said nothing at all in reply to her question.

She reached the forest again, where Suśaṅkha stayed;
then, out of wickedness, the best of ascetics was struck with blows of her hand.

When Suśaṅkha was struck by the daughter of Mṛtyu, O brāhmaṇas,
then, enraged, of great splendor, he cursed the slender-waisted girl:

"Since, O wicked one, I was struck by you although blameless,
while I was staying here in the forest, therefore I pronounce a curse:

Listen: when, entering householdership along with a husband,
a son full of sinful conduct, a slanderer of gods and brāhmaṇas,

devoted to all sins, O wicked one, will be in your womb!"
Having cursed her thus, he too departed and took resort to penance alone.

When that fortunate one had gone, Sunīthā went home,
and with an anguished mind told her great-souled father.

How she was cursed then by that son of a Gandharva—
all that, recounted by her, was heard by Mṛtyu.

[Mṛtyu said:] "Why was a blow struck by you against one who performs penance and is free from fault?
It was not proper, daughter, to strike a truthful one.

Having spoken thus, righteous Mṛtyu became exceedingly grieved,
reflecting upon her destiny in this manner.

Sūta said: The majestic son of Atri, famous and named Aṅga,
once went, O brāhmaṇas, to the Nandana garden, that twice-born one.

Seeing there the king of gods, Indra, the chastiser of Pāka,
accompanied by hosts of apsarases, and by Gandharvas and Kinnaras,

being sung to by singers in the seven pleasant notes,
and all fanned with fragrant fans,

by women endowed with beauty, with chowries moving like swans,
with an umbrella white as a swan, resembling the orb of the moon,

shining, the thousand-eyed one, adorned with all ornaments,
he saw that god of immeasurable splendor engaged in amorous play;

at his side the highly fortunate daughter of Puloman, charming and auspicious,
glorious through beauty, splendor, and asceticism,

shining with good fortune and devotion to her husband, that chaste woman;
with her, the thousand-eyed one sported in the Nandana grove.

Beholding his sport, Aṅga, the best of the twice-born, [thought:]
"Fortunate indeed is this king of gods, surrounded by such attendants!

Ah, the power of his penance, by which such a great station has been attained!
When such a son, the upholder of all the worlds,

should be mine, then I will attain great happiness here, there is no doubt!"
Thus immersed in thought, he returned home in haste.

2.31.m:
Sūta said: Then Aṅga, of great splendor, having seen the fortune of Indra,
and his enjoyment, amusement, and the sport of that great-souled one, [thought:]

"How might I have a son equal to Indra and endowed with righteousness?"
Having reflected for a moment, Aṅga, the foremost of upholders of dharma,

that Aṅga, devoted to truth, arrived at his own home,
bowed down with neck bent low, and asked his father Atri:

"Who is this who, through righteous conduct, enjoys great Indra-hood?
By the development of what merit? What deed was done, and of what kind?

What kind of penance was his? Whom did he worship in the past?
Tell me this in detail, O foremost of the truthful!"

Atri said: "Well said, well said, O fortunate one, since you ask me thus;
hear, my child, as I narrate the story of Indra!

Formerly there was an intelligent, excellent brāhmaṇa named Suvrata;
by him Kṛṣṇa Hṛṣīkeśa was propitiated through austerity.

He entered a holy womb from Kaśyapa through Aditi, indeed,
and by the grace of Viṣṇu he became the king of the gods."

Aṅga said: "How could I have a son equal to Indra, O you who are affectionate to your son?
Explain to me the means for that, for you are the foremost among the wise."

Atri said: "In brief, the entire meritorious life of that great-souled
Suvrata, hear, O you of great intellect!

How the wise Suvrata formerly propitiated Hari,
and the disposition, devotion, and meditation of that great-souled one."
Having observed [him], the Lord of the World granted indeed a supreme station— / the three worlds, moving and unmoving, endowed with all enjoyments, together with Indra.
And by the grace of Viṣṇu alone, he who sustains the three worlds enjoys the station. / Thus has everything of the conduct of Indra also been related to you.
Govinda is pleased by devotion, O best of beings, by meditation with feeling; / his mind satisfied, Hari, gratified by devotion, gives everything.
Therefore, having worshipped Govinda—the giver of all, the source of all, / the omniscient one, the knower of all, the supreme person of all—
from him you shall obtain whatever you desire, O delight.
He is the giver of happiness, the giver of the supreme goal, the giver of liberation, indeed the lord of the worlds. / Therefore, go worship him, my son; you will indeed obtain a son equal to Indra.
Having heard the speech endowed with the supreme truth spoken by the benevolent sage, / grasping the essence of his words, the great-souled one bowed to that eternal one and departed.
Having taken leave of his father, the son of Brahmā equal to Brahmā himself, the great-souled Aṅga / reached the peak of Mount Meru, joined with golden and jeweled [heights].

2.32.m: Sūta said: / With its body brightly shining with various jewels and also with gold on every side, / that best of mountains blazed forth like the sun with its rays.
Finding cool, happiness-granting shade beneath the Aśoka trees, / all the yogins meditate, seated on firm postures.
In some places ascetics perform austerities, in other places Kinnaras sing, / and satisfied sages and Gandharvas are active with lutes and rhythms.
Absorbed in tempo, measure, and rhythm, accompanied by the seven musical notes, / distinct and enchanting songs are sung, joined with melodic variations and pauses.
Indeed, taking shelter in the shade of sandalwood trees on that best of mountains, / Gandharvas, knowers of the true nature of music, devotedly sing songs.
There women of the gods dance upon the excellent mountain, / which destroys sin, bestows merit, is divine, and is the granter of highest welfare.
The melodious sound of the Veda is heard on that best of mountains; / with sandalwood, Aśoka, Punnāga, Śāla, palm, and Tamāla trees,
and with banyan trees resembling clouds, that excellent mountain shines forth; / crowded with Saṃtānaka and wish-fulfilling trees, and plantain trees,
the king of mountains shines everywhere with heavenly trees in full bloom. / Strewn with various minerals, the mountain is a heap of varied jewels.
Filled with various wonders, endowed with various auspicious things, / well frequented by assemblies of Vedic scholars, and crowded with hosts of Apsarases,
it shines brilliantly with ṛṣis, ascetics, Siddhas, and Gandharvas; / it blazes forth with elephants resembling mountains and with the roars of lions.
It is adorned with Śarabhas, rutting tigers, and crafty deer, / and with oblong tanks, wells, and pools filled with pure water.
Crowded with swans and Kāraṇḍava ducks, it is splendid everywhere, / and it shines with golden lotuses, white lotuses, and red lotuses.
With masses of flowing rivers and likewise with clear waters, / and with forms of Śāla and palm trees, and with elephants and crystal,
and filled with vast, divine golden rock surfaces radiant like the sun and fire, / the king of mountains shines resplendent.
Adorned with the celestial chariots of deities and mountain-like palaces / resembling swans and the moon, with golden flagstaffs,
embellished with palaces furnished with pinnacles and fly-whisks, / and beautified by hosts of gods rejoicing in various virtues,
and by numerous hosts of gods, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas, / the sacred Meru, best of excellent mountains, shines everywhere.
From it sprang the most holy Gaṅgā, the great river of holy water, / rich in holy bathing places, crowded with swans and lotuses.
That great river is frequented by ascetics and multitudes of sages. / Unto that best of mountains of such qualities, holy, wondrous, and auspicious,
the holy, great ascetic Aṅga, son of Atri, entered, / upon the holy banks of the Gaṅgā, in a solitary, delightful cave.
Sitting there, the wise man, freed from desire and anger, / restraining all his senses, set his mind upon Hṛṣīkeśa.
That righteous-minded one, meditating on Kṛṣṇa, the lord who removes afflictions, / [beheld] Madhusūdana while sitting, sleeping, walking, and in meditation.
Constantly he sees him, his self controlled, joined in yoga, senses subdued; / he perceives Keśava in moving and unmoving beings,
in moist things and in dry things, and in all other things, that noble twice-born one. / In this way a hundred years passed while he was practicing austerities.
Observing that best of the twice-born, the Lord of the World holding the discus in hand / constantly showed many very terrible obstacles.
Through the splendor of that divine, great-souled Nṛsiṃha, / that righteous-minded one, devoid of fear, burns them as fire burns fuel.
Through observances, restraints, and other fasts, that best of the twice-born, / though becoming emaciated, blazed forth with his own splendor.
Aṅga thus appeared resembling the sun and fire. / While he was thus deeply devoted to austerities and meditating upon Janārdana,
the God manifested and said, “Choose a boon, O giver of honor.” / And seeing Hṛṣīkeśa, Aṅga was exceedingly gladdened.
Bowing low with a clear mind, he praised Vāsudeva.
Aṅga said: / You are the refuge of all beings, O source of beings, O purifier! / O Soul of beings, Lord of all beings, salutation to you whose self is the qualities!
Salutation to you who have qualities as form, the secret one, the one transcending qualities; / to the quality, the maker of qualities, rich in qualities, the soul of qualities.
To existence, the maker of existence, the remover of mundane existence for devotees, / the source of existence, the secret one, salutation to the destroyer of mundane existence!
Salutation, salutation to the sacrifice, to the form of sacrifice, to the Lord of sacrifice; / to the connection of the sacrificial rite, and salutation to the bearer of the conch!
Salutation, salutation to the golden one; salutation to the bearer of the discus; / to the true, to the true state, and to the one consisting entirely of truth!
To dharma, to the maker of dharma, and to the maker of all, salutation to you; / to the one whose limbs are dharma, to the very heroic one, salutation to the support of dharma!
Salutation to the holy one, to the son, and to the sonless one, to the great-souled one; / to the destroyer of delusion caused by illusion, to you, the maker of all illusion!
To the bearer of illusion, to the embodied, and to the unembodied, salutation, salutation; / to the one bearing all forms, to Śaṃkara, salutation, salutation!
To Brahman, to the form of Brahman, to the one whose essential nature is the supreme Brahman; / salutation to you, the abode of all, and salutation to the upholder of the abode!
To the glorious one, to the dwelling place of Śrī, to Śrīdhara, salutation, salutation; / to the dweller in the ocean of milk, and salutation to you, the nectar of immortality!
To the great medicine, to the terrible, and to the one devoted to supreme wisdom; / to the non-cruel, to the highly sacrificial, salutation to the lord of sacrificial offerings!
To the endless, indeed to the complete, and salutation to the sinless one; / to the illumination of space, salutation to you in the form of a bird!

To the offered, to the enjoyer of the offering, and salutation to you in the form of sacrificial oblation; / to the enlightened, to the one whose form is the wise, salutation to you who are always awakened!
Salutation to the oblation to gods, to the oblation to ancestors, salutation to the utterance svadhā; / to the utterance svāhā, to the pure, to the unmanifest, to the great-souled one!
To Vyāsa, to Vāsava, and salutation to you whose form is the Vasus; / to Vāsudeva, to the universe, salutation to you whose form is fire; / to Hari, to the absolute, salutation, salutation to Vāmana!
Praise to the divine Nṛsiṃha, praise to You, the protector of living beings!
Praise to Govinda, to Gopāla, and praise to the single syllable; / praise indeed to the universal syllable, praise to You whose form is the Haṃsa!
Praise to You who are the three principles, praise to You who are the five principles, / praise indeed to You who are the twenty-five principles, to the foundation of the principles!
Praise to Kṛṣṇa, to Him whose form is dark, to the lord of Lakṣmī; / praise to Him who is like a lotus petal, to supreme bliss!
Praise to the supporter of the universe, praise indeed to the destroyer of sin; / praise to pure merit, praise to You whose dharma is truth!
Praise, praise to the eternal, the imperishable; praise, praise to the one whose nature is the compact sky! / To the venerable Padmanābha, the Great Lord, I bow, to the lotus feet of Keśava!

O root of bliss, beloved of Kamalā, O Vāsudeva, Lord of all, Master, Madhusūdana, grant me servitorship! / I bow to Your feet, O Keśava, birth after birth; have mercy on me, O giver of peace, conch-holder!

Consumed by the dreadful fire of worldly existence, by the deaths of sons and relatives and by many torments of grief, / inundate me with the rain-cloud of knowledge, O Padmanābha! Be the refuge of this wretched person, O Lord!
Having thus heard the praise spoken even by the noble Aṅga, / He displayed His own form, dark as a storm-cloud and of immense power,
holding a conch, discus, and mace in His hands, with a lotus in His hand, the great Sovereign. / His own form, mounted upon Garuḍa, was revealed,
His limbs adorned with every ornament—with necklaces, bracelets, and earrings— / shining, supreme, divine, pure with a garland of forest flowers.
Before Aṅga, Hṛṣīkeśa stood shining with great splendor, / Janārdana, marked with the holy Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem.
Having shown His own body, Hari, who consists of all gods, / spoke to that noble one, to Aṅga, the best of sages:
“O noble Brahmin, listen to my auspicious words!” / Addressing the best of the twice-born with a voice deep as a thundercloud,
“I am pleased by this austerity of yours; choose an auspicious boon!” / Seeing Hṛṣīkeśa, the husband of Kamalā, thus pleased,
blazing, radiant, the universal form, the lord of people, / bowing again and again at His two lotus feet,
filled with immense joy, he spoke to Janārdana: / “I am Your servant, O Lord of gods, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace!
If You desire to give me a boon, grant me a son born of my lineage, / who shines like Indra in heaven, endowed with all splendor.
Grant me such a son, a protector of all the world, / dear to all gods, O God, devoted to Brahmins, learned in dharma,
generous, endowed with wisdom, accompanied by the splendor of dharma, / a protector of the three worlds, O Kṛṣṇa, an upholder of true dharma,
the foremost among sacrificers, unique, heroic, an ornament of the three worlds, / devoted to Brahmins, learned in the Veda, true to his word, with senses subdued,
unconquered, conqueror of all, equal in brilliance to the splendor of Viṣṇu, / a Vaiṣṇava, a performer of meritorious deeds, born of merit, marked by auspicious signs,
tranquil, endowed with austerity, skilled in all scriptures, / knowledgeable in the Veda, the best of yogins, and resembling You in virtues.
Grant me such a son, since You desire to give a boon.” / The blessed Vāsudeva said: “Endowed with these qualities, a son shall be born to you,
the supporter of the lineage of Atri, of this whole world, O wise one! / Through his splendor, fame, and merits, he will deliver his father.
He who shall deliver his father and grandfather through his truths, / and you shall go to my abode, that highest step of Viṣṇu.”
Having said this, the lord of the gods [spoke] to that Aṅga, O good twice-born: / "Marry the virtuous daughter of someone of meritorious valor."
Beget upon her an auspicious, beloved son who brings merit; / by my grace he will be righteous, O wise one,
all-knowing and all-perceiving, just as desired by you.” / Having thus granted the boon, Hari disappeared.

2.33.m: The sages said: / “Cursed by the noble Suśaṅkha, the son of a Gandharva, / how was she born from his curse, and what deed was done by her?
What kind of son did she obtain through his curse, O best of the twice-born? / Tell us in detail the deeds of Sunīthā.”
Sūta said: / “Cursed indeed by that Suśaṅkha, that slender-waisted woman, / afflicted by grief, Sunīthā went to her father's abode.
Her conduct was revealed by her to her father. / That righteous Mṛtyu, foremost among the truthful, also heard it.
He spoke to Sunīthā, his daughter cursed by the noble one: / ‘A wicked sin destroying the splendor of dharma has been committed by you.
Why was the striking of that tranquil one done by you, O fortunate one? / An action opposed to all the world has been devised by you.
He is free from desire and anger, very tranquil, affectionate toward dharma, / dissolved in the path of austerity, and established in the Supreme Brahman.
Hear the sin of whoever strikes such a person: / a sinful son is born to them, and they incur much fault.
Whoever strikes one who does not strike back, or abuses one who does not abuse, / incurs the sin of the one who was struck, there is no doubt.
He indeed is tranquil, self-conquered, who does not strike back at one striking him. / By whomsoever a beating is inflicted upon an innocent person, O daughter,
and afterwards strikes an innocent person out of delusion and sin, / by whomsoever heartache is caused vainly to an innocent person,
and afterwards strikes an innocent person out of delusion and through some sin, / that sinner incurs the bodily sin of the innocent one.
Or if the innocent one should kill that striking, evil-minded person, / rising up quickly with force and boldness against that evil-minded one,
the sin belonging to the wrongdoer goes to the innocent person. / Therefore, striking should not be done even against one who is at fault.
And a great wickedness has been harbored by you alone, O daughter, / since you were cursed by him this very day; therefore, practice merit.
Having obtained the company of the virtuous, conduct yourself always [accordingly]; / through the yoga of meditation and knowledge, conduct yourself, O daughter!
The company of the virtuous yields great merit and brings about much welfare. / O child, see the good example showing the quality of association with the virtuous:
from touching, drinking, and bathing in water, sages of great intelligence / attain perfection, cleansed within and without.
All these worlds, moving and unmoving, become purified by it. / Waters are tranquil, very cool, soft to the touch, and pleasing,
pure, full of essence, possessing holy power, and removing impurities. / In the same way, the virtuous should be recognized by you and served with effort.
Just as gold sheds its impurity through contact with fire, / so through association with the virtuous does a mortal shed sin.
The fire of truth is ignited and blazes with the brilliance of merit; / blazing in brilliance through truth, it is also completely pure through knowledge,
extremely hot through the condition of meditation, untouchable by men born of sin. / Through contact with the fire of truth, all sin is destroyed.
Therefore, you must by all means cultivate association with truth; / having abandoned the burden of sin, take refuge in merit in this way!’”

Sūta said:
Thus enlightened by her father, the sorrowful Sunīthā,
having bowed down to her father's feet, went to the solitary forest.

Abandoning desire, anger, and childhood ways, the ascetic girl,
having renounced delusion, malice, and deceit, took resort to seclusion.

Her female friends arrived, full of playful sport, in order to play;
the large-eyed girls saw Sunīthā sharing in sorrow.

To her, meditating and anxious, they, filled with concern, said:
“Why do you worry, fair one, overwhelmed by this anxiety?

Tell us the cause; anxiety is a giver of pain.
Only one kind of anxiety is meaningful: that which is contemplated for the sake of dharma.

The second meaningful anxiety is that of yogins, delighting in dharma;
any other anxiety is useless—one should never entertain it.

Anxiety destroys the body, it destroys strength and splendor;
it ruins all happiness and causes loss of beauty.

Anxiety brings on craving, delusion, and greed;
anxiety creates sin when pondered day after day.

Anxiety leads to the manifestation of disease and prepares one for hell.
Therefore, having cast aside anxiety, pursue [life with us], fair one.

Whatever has been previously acquired by a person through their own action,
that very thing does this living being experience; a wise person should not worry.

Therefore, abandon anxiety, and speak of pleasure, pain, and the like.”
Having heard their words, Sunīthā spoke these words.

2.34.m:
Sūta said:
How she had been cursed in the forest previously by the great-souled Suśaṅkha,
all that conduct she related to those friends.

And the illustrious girl, deeply afflicted with grief,
Sunīthā said: “I shall tell another thing too; friends, listen now.

Seeing my wealth of beauty, youth, and treasure of virtues,
my father became filled with anxiety on my account.

Desiring to give me to the gods or to sages, he, of great renown,
took me by the hand and spoke these words to them all:

‘This young daughter of mine possesses virtues and lovely eyes;
I wish to give her to a virtuous, great-souled one; auspiciousness to you!’

The gods and sages then heard the speech of Mṛtyu;
led by Indra, those gods spoke to him as he was speaking:

‘This daughter of yours is rich in virtues, a supreme treasury of good conduct;
yet she is corrupted by a single fault: by that curse of the sage.

Whatever son will be born from her by a man's seed,
he will indeed be a great sinner, the destroyer of a meritorious lineage.

A pot is seen completely filled with Gaṅgā water,
yet if smeared with a drop of wine, it becomes a wine-pot.

From the association with the sin of a sinful one, the whole family becomes sinful.
If a drop of sour gruel falls into the midst of milk,
Afterward it ruins the milk and reveals its own nature; / in like manner, a sinful son destroys the lineage, without doubt.

Even by this fault, this girl of yours has become a sharer in sin;
go, let her be given to someone else.’ Thus was my father addressed by the gods.

And forsaken by the gods, gandharvas, and great-souled sages,
my father was oppressed with sorrow.

Good people, too, do not accept me;
such a sinful act was done by me in the past.

Tormented with pain and grief, I have taken refuge in the forest;
I will perform penance and dry up my body.

I was rightly asked by you about the cause of the matter;
my deed that led to my anxiety has been revealed to you by me.”

Having spoken thus, Sunīthā, the renowned daughter of Mṛtyu,
pained with sorrow, fell silent and said nothing more.

Her friends said:
“O illustrious one, abandon this grief that destroys the body!
In whose family is there no fault? Sin has been resorted to [even] by the gods.

In the past, deceit was spoken by Brahmā in the presence of Hara;
yet although forsaken by the gods, Brahmā became the most worthy of worship.

Look, oh! Even the king of the gods, affected by the killing of a brāhmaṇa,
enjoys the three worlds along with the gods, illustrious one.

In the past, he went to Ahalyā, the beloved wife of Gautama;
though an adulterer with another's wife, he remains in divine status.

Hara committed a dreadful act resembling the killing of a brāhmaṇa,
and even today he wanders with the skull of Brahmā.

The gods and the sages versed in the Vedas bow to that god.
The Sun, afflicted with leprosy, illuminates the three worlds.

The beings beginning with the gods, with the moving and unmoving, bow to that god.
Kṛṣṇa experiences the great curse made in the past by Bhārgava.

The Moon went to his guru's wife and because of that became consumptive;
yet he will be of great splendor, a king of kings, powerful.

The son of Pāṇḍu, highly wise, righteous Yudhiṣṭhira,
will speak an untruth for the sake of slaying his guru.

In these very ones and among great persons great sin exists;
who indeed has no flaw? Who has no blemish?

You are stained with only a slight fault, fair-faced one;
we shall render assistance to you, fair-complexioned girl.

The virtues that exist in your limbs, such as belong to true women, auspicious one,
those virtues we do not see elsewhere, beautiful-eyed one.

Beauty is the first virtue and ornament of women, auspicious one;
good conduct is the second, and truth is the third.

Straightforwardness is the fourth, and dharma is indeed the fifth;
sweetness is declared as the sixth, fair-faced one.

Purity inside and out among women is the seventh, young girl;
devotion to the father is the eighth, and service is indeed the ninth.

Patience is proclaimed as the tenth, and pleasure as the eleventh;
devotion to the husband is then proclaimed as the twelfth, fair-complexioned one.

Adorned with these you are, young girl; do not fear, fair-faced one!
By whichever means your husband will be an upholder of noble dharma,

that means we ourselves shall see for your sake.”
Those excellent friends said to her: “Do not take rash action!”

Sūta said:
Addressed thus, Sunīthā, praised by her friends, spoke again:
“Tell me the means by which there will be a husband.”

Those excellent women, Rambhā and the others, lovely-eyed,
said to her: “Endowed with beauty and charm, you increase prosperity.

Terrified by the brāhmaṇa's curse, we have gathered here.”
And they said to the large-eyed, fair-eyed daughter of Mṛtyu:

“We will give you a spell that fascinates men,
a giver of all good things, fair one, known to those skilled in all magical crafts.”

Then they gave her the power of the spell that bestows happiness:
“Whomever you wish to enchant, fair one—gods and so forth—

instantly enchant him!” Addressed thus, she did so.
When the spell was fully mastered, Sunīthā was greatly delighted.

She roamed with her female friends, looking at men;
wandering, she came to the holy, excellent Nandana forest.

Then, seeing a brāhmaṇa on the bank of the Gaṅgā endowed with handsome form,
endowed with all auspicious marks, of radiance equal to the sun's splendor—
In beauty peerless in the world, like a second Manmatha, / possessing a divine form, highly fortunate, prosperous, bestowing good fortune,
incomparable, high-souled, shining with radiance like that of Viṣṇu, / a Vaiṣṇava, destroying all sins, endowed with valor equal to Viṣṇu's,
free from desire and anger, an ornament of the lineage of Atri.

Seeing him of fair form, the very embodiment of austerities, divine in majesty, practicing penance, / filled with passion she asked her dear friend Rambhā: “Who is this foremost high-souled one dwelling in heaven?”

2.35.m: Rambhā said: / Brahmā arose from the Unmanifest; from him was born the Prajāpati / named Atri, righteous-minded; his son is high-minded.
This is he, named Aṅga, fair lady, who has come to the Nandana forest. / Having seen the prosperity of Indra, the supreme sport and splendor,
he too formed a longing for a rank equal to Indra's: / “If only I had a son like this, endowed with righteousness,
my birth would be truly auspicious, attended with fame and renown!” / Thus Hṛṣīkeśa was propitiated by austerities and observances.
When Hṛṣīkeśa was well pleased, he asked for a boon: / “A son equal to Indra, with the splendor and prowess of Viṣṇu,
a Vaiṣṇava, destroying all sins—grant him to me, O Madhusūdana!” / Then he granted him such a son, the upholder of all.
From that time forward the best of Brahmins looks out for a meritorious maiden; / as you are lovely in all your limbs, so he looks around.
Go to him, O fair-hipped lady; from him a son will be born, / meritorious of soul, knowing righteous duties, possessing the splendor and prowess of Viṣṇu.
All this has been told to you as I was asked by you. / He is a worthy husband for you; there should be no doubt about it.
Even the curse of Suśaṅkha will also come to naught / when a highly fortunate son who promotes righteousness is born from him.
You will be happy, fair lady; I speak the absolute truth. / When a farmer diligently sows seed in a good field,
he enjoys it accordingly, O divine lady: as the seed is, so is the fruit. / It would never happen otherwise; everything corresponds to it.
He is this highly fortunate ascetic of virtuous vigor; / born from his semen, endowed with the abundance of his very qualities,
a son of great splendor, the foremost among all embodied beings, / will be highly fortunate, composed in mind, knowing the truth of yoga.

Having heard those words spoken by dear Rambhā, which bestowed auspiciousness, / the young girl Sunīthā, having considered this essential matter with her intellect, [concluded] that it was indeed true.

2.36.m: Sunīthā said: / You have spoken the truth, fair lady; I shall do this. / By this artifice I will bewitch the Brahmin, not otherwise.
Give me holy assistance, so that I may go at once. / Thus spoken to by her, Rambhā said to that determined woman:
What kind of assistance shall I give? Tell me the truth, O passionate lady! / “Act as my messenger right now, fair lady, toward him.”
Thus it was spoken by her to that fair-eyed Rambhā; / exactly so was it promised by Rambhā, the divine woman:
“I will give you assistance; let my command be given [by you].” / With sincere intention, the large-eyed lady, endowed with beauty and youth,
by illusion became of divine form, fair of face, / peerless in beauty in the world, enchanting the three worlds.
And on a most sacred peak of Meru, in a beautiful cave / filled with various minerals and adorned with various gems,
filled with divine trees, adorned with many flowers, / crowded with hosts of gods, frequented by Gandharvas and Apsarases,
charming and delightful, filled with cool shade / of sandalwood and aśoka trees, the sweet-smiling lady,
mounted upon a swing, adorned with all ornaments, / radiant in fine dark-blue silk, fair of face,
with a bodice the color of a bandhūka flower, O best of Brahmins, / the maiden beautiful in every limb, her hands engaged with the lute and rhythm,
singing an excellent song with a sweet melody, bewitching the universe, / surrounded by those friends, the most charming girl [sat].
Meanwhile Aṅga, in a sacred cave, had sat down in solitude in meditation; / free from desire and anger, he was meditating upon Janārdana.
Hearing the sweet, very delightful singing with its fine melody, / accompanied by rhythm and measure, captivating all living beings,
the radiant one wavered from meditation, enchanted by the illusory song. / Rising quickly from his seat, looking repeatedly,
he went there in haste, his mind agitated by the illusion. / Seeing her seated on the swing, her hands busy with the neck of the lute,
smiling, singing sweetly, her face like the full moon, / the illustrious one was bewitched by that song and also by her beauty.
By the charm of her loveliness, struck by the arrows of Manmatha, / his understanding troubled and bewildered, the sage's son, best of Brahmins,
babbled through intense infatuation and yawned again and again; / sweat, trembling, and fever arose in him that very moment.
As if fainting under profound delusions, languid, his mind wavering, / trembling and tormented, Aṅga then approached.
Seeing that large-eyed lady, the renowned daughter of Mṛtyu, / that high-souled one then said to Sunīthā of the charming smile:
“Who are you, whose [daughter], O fair-hipped one, surrounded by friends? / For what purpose have you arrived, [and] by whom were you sent to the forest?
Your whole body is beautiful and shines here in the great forest. / Explain to me this very day; be gracious, O fair-faced lady!”
Utterly deluded by the infatuation of illusion, he did not know her deed; / pierced deeply by the arrows of Manmatha, the great sage
having heard such an important statement of the high-minded one, / she said nothing to the Brahmin, looking toward the face of her friend.
And Sunīthā urged her friend Rambhā with a gesture; / then Rambhā spoke respectfully to that Brahmin:
“This maiden is highly fortunate, [daughter] of the high-souled Mṛtyu; / she is famed as Sunīthā, endowed with all auspicious marks.
The maiden is seeking a husband who is righteous, a treasury of austerities, / tranquil, self-controlled, very wise, and skilled in the knowledge of the Vedas.”
Having heard such an important statement, the great sage, / Aṅga, then said to her, to Rambhā, the foremost of Apsarases:
“Viṣṇu, Hari consisting of the entire universe, was worshipped by me; / by him a boon was granted to me, named a son, who bestows all success.
For that reason, fair lady, for the sake of a son, I am constantly / seeking a maiden of some man of virtuous vigor.
I had never seen such a truly good wife. / This fair-faced girl is the daughter of Dharma, observing righteous conduct.
Let her indeed accept me, if she desires a husband here; / whatever this young girl may desire, I shall grant it, no doubt.”
[He said,] “Even what should not be given will be given for the sake of union with her.” / “Only one thing must be given by you; listen, O best of Brahmins.”
Rambhā said: / “O best of Brahmins, listen here to the promise I now speak: / she must never be abandoned by you, for she is your lawful wife.”
"You must never take note of any fault or virtue in her. / In this matter, O twice-born, show me a visible pledge.
Give your hand, O best of twice-borns, to produce a true guarantee." / [The king said:] "So be it; her hand is indeed taken by me, without doubt."
Sūta said: / Having thus made an alliance that produced a true pledge, / he married Sunīthā by the gāndharva rite.
Having given Sunīthā to him with a delighted heart, / Rambhā, taking leave of her, went back to her own home.
Her friends, with delighted hearts, departed to their own abode. / When all those friends had departed, the best of the twice-born,
Aṅga, sported together with her, his beloved wife. / Having begotten on her a son endowed with all auspicious marks,
he gave that very son the name Vena. / Then that son of Sunīthā, endowed with great splendor, grew up.
Having studied the Vedic scriptures and the archery manual full of virtues, / the intelligent boy reached the end of all sciences.
Vena, the son of Aṅga, conducted himself according to the conduct of the virtuous; / that best of brāhmaṇas, Vena, became devoted to the conduct of a kṣatriya.
Just as Indra shines in heaven, endowed with all majesty, / so the very wise [prince] shone through his own strength and heroic deeds.
When the interval of Cākṣuṣa had passed and [the Manu period] of Vaivasvata had arrived, / the subjects in the world were continually suffering without a protector of the people.
The ṛṣis, knowers of the truth of dharma whose wealth was penance, for the sake of the subjects / contemplated an earthly ruler who knew dharma and was learned in truth.
They saw that very Vena, endowed and accompanied by auspicious marks; / the best of twice-borns consecrated him to the sacred station of ruler of subjects.
When that illustrious king, the son of Aṅga, was consecrated, / all those lords of subjects departed to the forest of penance.
When they had all departed, Vena ruled the kingdom. / Sūta said: / Sunīthā, having seen her son establishing order over the entire kingdom,
doubted on account of the power of that great soul's curse: / "Will my son, fortunate though he is, be a protector of dharma?"
Thus one should constantly reflect, apprehensive because of past sin; / one should display the very virtuous limbs of dharma before one's son.
she revealed to him the meritorious virtues such as truthfulness and the rest. / For she said to her son: "O son, I am the daughter of Dharma;
your father knows the essence of dharma; therefore, practice dharma!" / In this way the virtuous woman constantly instructed her son Vena.
He obeyed the words of his parents, which were beneficial to the subjects. / Thus Vena became a protector of subjects on the surface of the earth.
The world lived in happiness; the subjects were pleased by dharma. / Such was the power of the reign of that noble-minded Vena,
and dispositions toward dharma prevailed while that king ruled.

2.37.m: The ṛṣis said: / Such was the conduct of the noble-minded Vena; / how then, abandoning the conduct of dharma, did he become evil-minded?
Sūta said: / Sages endowed with knowledge and discernment, knowers of truth, / speak of good and evil in this way, and here it cannot be otherwise.
How could a curse given by that noble-minded Suśaṅkha, / even as he was performing penance, turn out otherwise, O twice-borns?
I shall tell you all about Vena's sinful conduct. / While that noble-minded protector of subjects who knew dharma was ruling,
a certain man arrived, wearing a deceptive guise, / of naked appearance, with a huge body, a shaved head, and great brilliance,
carrying a broom of peacock feathers in his armpit, / and holding a drinking bowl made of coconut in his hand,
reciting an unrighteous scripture that reviles the Vedic dharma. / He came in haste to where the great king Vena was.
That sinful one entered the assembly of that Vena; / having seen him arrive, Vena then asked a question:
"Who are you that have arrived, bearing such an appearance? / Why have you come before me as I sit in the assembly?
What is this guise? What is your name? What is your dharma? State your work! / What is your Veda? What is your conduct? What is your penance? What is your teaching?
What is your knowledge? What is your power? What is truth, and what is the mark of dharma? / Declare all the reality before me, and only the truth!"
Having heard those words of Vena, the wicked one spoke: / The sinner said: / "You rule the kingdom in vain; you are greatly foolish, without a doubt.
I am the all-in-all of dharma; I am most worshipped by the gods. / I am knowledge, I am truth, I am the eternal Creator;
I am dharma, I am liberation, I am composed of all deities. / Arisen from the body of Brahmā, I am true to my vow, not otherwise.
Know me to be the form of Jina, the embodiment of true dharma; / indeed, yogins devoted to knowledge run only toward me."
Vena said: / "Of what kind is your action, and what is your philosophical view? / What is your conduct? Speak, come!"—thus was he addressed by that king.
The sinner said: / "Where Arhat is the deity, where a Nirgrantha is seen as the teacher, / and where compassion is the highest dharma, there liberation is seen.
In this doctrine, without a doubt, I proclaim the rules of conduct: / there is no sacrificing, no officiating at sacrifices, nor any recitation of the Vedas;
there is no twilight worship, penance, or gift, and it is devoid of the svadhā and svāhā calls; / there is no offering to gods or ancestors, nor any action such as Vedic sacrifice;
there is no libation to the ancestors, no reception of guests, and no Vaiśvadeva rite; / excellent worship of the ascetic and supreme meditation on the Arhat [are prescribed].
This practice of dharma is seen in the Jain path. / All this has been declared to you as the characteristic mark of my own dharma."
Vena said: / "In dharma as proclaimed by the Vedas, in which actions such as sacrifices exist, / the libation to ancestors, the śrāddha, and the Vaiśvadeva are not missing;
nor are gifts or penance absent. Where is the mark of your dharma? / Speak the truth before me: of what kind is this dharma of compassion?"
The sinner said: / "This body of living beings is grown from the five elements, / and the self is in the form of wind; there is no lasting connection among them.
Just as the union of physical elements in water / arises in the form of a bubble, so is the combination of the elements.
The earth-element is present in the dust, and the waters reside there; / fire is perceived therein, and good wind is present in the three;
space encloses them afterward, and the bubble-state is produced. / In the midst of the waters shines that excellent, round, and splendid form;
for merely a moment it is seen, and after a moment it is seen no more. / In that same way the conjunction of elements is observed everywhere.
At the time of death the self departs, and the five [elements] dissolve into the five. / Deluded by infatuation, mortals then interact with one another;
through delusion they perform the śrāddha and the ancestral libation on the anniversary of death. / Where does the dead man abide? Does he eat? Of what sort is he, O best of kings?
What is knowledge? What kind of body [is it]? By whom has it been seen? Tell us! / And having been fed sweet food, the brāhmaṇas depart satisfied:
to whom is the śrāddha given? That faith is entirely useless! / I shall tell you something else: the cruel ritual of the Vedas."
When a guest comes to the house, the brahmin cooks a great ox / or a goat, O king of kings, and feeds the guest.
In the horse sacrifice they kill a horse, and in the cow sacrifice a bull; / in the human sacrifice a man, O king, and likewise in the Vājapeya goats.
In the Rājasūya, O great king, there is much slaughter of living beings; / in the Puṇḍarīka one slaughters an elephant, and in the elephant sacrifice an elephant.
In the Sautrāmaṇī a sacrificial victim—a ram—is seen. / Listen, O son of the king, regarding all these manifold rites:
The slaughter of animals of various distinct species is prescribed [in the Vedas]; / and as for the gift that is given, what is the nature of that gift?
That food is to be known as leftover scraps, though abundant eating takes place; / and they kill those very animals devoid of any fault in the great sacrifice.
What righteousness is seen there, what fruit is there, O ruler of the earth, / where the slaughter of animals is prescribed by scholars of the Veda?
Therefore, it is ruined righteousness, not merit granting liberation; / for whatever righteousness lacks compassion becomes completely fruitless.
Where the protection of living beings is, there is righteousness, without a doubt. / The exclamation svāhā, the exclamation svadhā, asceticism, and truth, O best of kings—
devoid of compassion, they become fickle, and there is no righteousness there at all. / These Vedas are not Vedas where compassion is not found.
One devoted constantly to compassion and gifts, who protects living beings— / be he even a Cāṇḍāla or a Śūdra—he alone is called a brahmin.
A brahmin who is merciless, devoted to the slaughter of animals— / he indeed is pitiless, sinful, hard-hearted, and cruel-minded.
The Veda that is devoid of knowledge was proclaimed by deceivers; / where true knowledge is always present, there the Veda is established.
When the Vedas and the brahmins are devoid of compassion, O intelligent one, / then there is no truth nor ritual action among those Vedas and brahmins.
The Vedas are not Vedas, O king of kings, and the brahmins are devoid of truth; / there is also no fruit of giving, so no gift should be given.
As is the mark of the funeral ceremony, so is the nature of the gift. / Moreover, as for the teaching of the Jina, which bestows enjoyment and liberation,
I shall proclaim it before you, as it bestows great merit: / first, compassion should be practiced with a mind that has become tranquil.
One should worship in one's heart the divine Jina, by whom the moving and unmoving world [is encompassed]; / with a mind endowed with pure devotion, one should worship the Jina alone.
Obeisance must be paid to that god, not otherwise; / and one must never bow down to the feet of parents.
What need to speak of others? Listen, O best of kings! / Vena said: “These brahmins, teachers, and rivers like the Gaṅgā
speak of sacred places and how they bestow great merit. / Tell me the truth about that, if you desire righteousness here.”
The sinful one said: “From the sky indeed, O great king, clouds rain down water; / on the ground, on mountains, everywhere water falls.
Washing himself in it, he should remain, contemplating compassion everywhere. / Rivers are streams of sin; how could a sacred place be heard of among them?
Reservoirs of water, O great king, ponds, and oceans, / and mountains supporting the earth, are merely heaps of stones.
There is no sacred place in these, nor is water the best giver of water. / If there were great merit in bathing, why would there not be [merit] in fish?
No perfection is seen by bathing; fish are not purified by anything else. / Where the Jina is, there is the sacred place, there is eternal righteousness.
Asceticism, giving, and all such merit is established there.

The Jina alone consists of everything, O king; there is no other supreme righteousness, no other sacred place! / This indeed is the supreme gain; therefore meditate constantly, and you will become exceedingly happy.”

Reviling all righteousness along with the Veda, and giving along with merit in the form of supreme sacrifices, / the king, the son of Aṅga, was instructed at length by that sinful, evil-natured one on earth.

2.38.m: Sūta said: / Thus instructed, Vena indeed turned to evil ways, / deluded by that very sinful Jaina man.
Having bowed at the feet of that wicked-minded person, / abandoning the righteousness of the Veda and the practice of truthfulness and the like,
a cessation of proper sacrifices occurred, as well as of the Vedas; / and the righteousness consisting of holy treatises was not promoted then at all.
The entire world became full of sin under his rule; / there were no sacrifices, no Vedas, and no excellent meaning of the legal treatises;
there was neither giving nor study, O brahmins, while that ruler governed the earth. / In this way, the destruction of righteousness took place, and great sin was set in motion.
Though restrained by Aṅga, he acted entirely contrary; / the wicked-minded one did not bow to the feet of his father, nor of his mother.
He [did not bow] to any brahmin, [saying,] 'I alone am powerful!' / Though restrained by his father and by his mother, the wicked-minded one
never performed auspicious, meritorious acts, sacred pilgrimages, giving, or the like; / and the renowned one [spent] a long time according to his own disposition.
Then, considering all this: 'Why was this sinner born, / this son of the progenitor Aṅga, who has become a blemish on the lineage?'
the righteous [Aṅga] asked the daughter of great-souled Mṛtyu again: / 'By whose fault was he born? Tell me the truth, my dear.'
Sunīthā said: / The daughter formerly told Aṅga her own story and her own merit: / 'It is through my fault, O noble-minded one.
In childhood, a sin was committed by me against the great-souled Suśaṅkha, / even while he was engaged in ascetic penance; nothing else was done by me.
Cursed was I by him as he grew angry: “May your offspring be wicked!” / Thus I know, O fortunate one, that because of that he has become wicked.'
Hearing this, the one of great splendor went with her to the forest. / When that fortunate one had gone to the forest with his wife at that time,
these seven sages went there to the side of Vena; / calling him forth, they addressed the son of Aṅga:
The sages said: / “Do not act rashly, Vena! Be a protector of the subjects here; / by you, all this world, the three worlds with moving and unmoving beings,
and all things, O fortunate one, are established in righteousness! / Abandoning sinful deeds, perform meritorious deeds.”
When they had spoken thus, he laughed and said these words: / Vena said: “I alone am the supreme righteousness; I alone am the eternal Arhat;
I am the Creator, I am the protector, and I am the meaning of the Vedas; / I am righteousness, great merit, the eternal Jaina doctrine!
Worship me alone through action, O brahmins, who am the embodiment of righteousness!” / The sages said: “Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are the three twice-born castes;
for all castes this revelation is eternal; / they conduct themselves by the Vedic practice, and by that living beings survive.
Born from the lineage of Brahmā, you are indeed a brahmin, / and later you became the king of the earth, endowed with prowess.
Through the merit of the king, O king of kings, the twice-born live happily; / through the sin of the king, they perish. Therefore, practice merit!
Righteousness was respected by you and practiced [in the past], O king of men; / neither the deed of the Tretā age nor of the Dvāpara age [should be neglected].”
Men will bring about the entrance of the Kali age, / taking recourse to the Jain religion, all deluded by sin.
Abandoning Vedic conduct, men will turn to sin; / indeed, the Jain religion is the root of sin, without doubt.
Bewildered by this, O king of kings, fallen through great delusion, / men are multitudes of sin; [he comes] for their destruction, not otherwise.
Govinda will surely appear, the remover of all sins; / assuming a form at his own will, he will destroy them from wickedness.
When [men] have thus sunk into sins, then for the destruction of the mlecchas / the lord will become none other than Kalki himself, without doubt.
Abandon the conduct of the Kali age and take refuge in merit; / conduct yourself according to truth and become a protector of subjects."
Vena said: / "I am the best of the wise; everything here is known by me. / Whoever behaves otherwise is certainly fit to be punished."
At the king of sinful mind who spoke thus excessively, / all those great-souled sons of Brahmā became enraged.
When the great-souled brāhmaṇas were thus angered, / King Vena entered an anthill out of fear of their brāhmaṇa curse.
Then those enraged sages looked for Vena in all directions. / Knowing that the king who had vanished was now situated in the anthill,
the brāhmaṇas dragged out that cruel one of sinful mind by force. / Seeing him of sinful deeds, the sages, highly composed,
churned the left arm of the king, having become furious. / From it was born an extremely short, blue-colored, terrifying [being],
a barbarian with red eyes, holding an arrow in his hand and bearing a bow. / He became the ancestor of all the sinful Niṣādas,
a creator and protector, a king especially for the mlecchas. / Seeing him of sinful deeds, the sages, O wise one,
churned the right arm of the high-souled Vena as well. / From it was born that great-souled one by whom the earth was milked,
named Pṛthu, greatly wise, a king of kings of great strength. / And by the favor of his merit, Vena, conversant with dharma and wealth,
having enjoyed the status of a universal monarch by the grace of the wielder of the discus, / went to the realm of Viṣṇu, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

2.39.m: The sages said: / "How did Vena go to heaven, having cast away sin far off? / Tell us that in detail here too, O best of the truthful."
Sūta said: / "From contact with the merit of the sages and from dialogue [with them], O best of the twice-born, / and through the churning of his body, the sin departed outside him.
Afterward, that Vena of virtuous soul attained eternal knowledge. / On the southern bank of the Revā, he performed austerities, O twice-born ones,
in the sin-destroying hermitage of the sage Tṛṇabindu, / for more than a hundred years, free from desire and anger.
By his fierce austerities the god bearing the conch, discus, and mace / became pleased, O illustrious ones, with the sinless king.
And he said: 'I am pleased; let an excellent boon be chosen.' / Vena said: 'If you are pleased, O god, grant me an excellent boon.
Even with this body I wish to go to your abode, / along with my father, O illustrious one, and with my mother, O lord of gods, / by your own splendor, O god, to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.'
The glorious Vāsudeva said: / 'Where has that great delusion gone by which you were deluded, O king, / cast into the path of darkness by greed attended by delusion?'
Vena said: / 'By whatever sin was committed by me previously, by that I was deluded, O lord. / Therefore deliver me from this and from very terrible sin.
Tell me out of grace, O lord, what is to be muttered or recited.' / The Blessed Lord said: 'Well done, O king! O fortunate one, your sin has come to an end;
and you are purified by austerity. Therefore I shall speak of the meritorious [hymn]. / Formerly indeed, my child, I was asked by Brahmā just as by you.
What was spoken to him, dear one, that whole [matter] I shall tell you. / Once, by Brahmā residing in meditation on the navel-lotus,
[I was seen] when I appeared to him then to bestow a boon, O one of good vows. / By him was asked a greatly meritorious hymn that destroys sins,
named Vāsudeva, wishing for that which bestows a good destination. / The highest of hymns, the great one called Vāsudeva,
which bestows all happiness to men who always recite and chant it, / causing great delight to Viṣṇu, I taught [to him], O fortunate one.
Viṣṇu said: / "All this world is pervaded by me, whose form is unmanifest; / therefore the sages devoted to Viṣṇu call me Viṣṇu.
In whom beings dwell, and who, all-pervading, dwells in them, / he is to be recognized with reverence by the wise as Vāsudeva, that is, I.
Since the all-pervading lord draws back the creatures at the end into the unmanifest, / therefore by those who have taken refuge he is to be known by the name Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Assuming any form at will upon an impulse, with the desire 'May I be many,' / therefore I am to be known by the wise seeking sons as Pradyumna.
In this world, except for the two lords of all, Hara and Keśava, / I am unobstructed by anyone by the power of yoga, hence Aniruddha.
I am named Viśva in each world, endowed with knowledge and discernment, / and the egotistic one, troubled by waking thoughts.
I am Taijasa, full of the world's activities and possessing the form of the senses, / abounding in knowledge and action, having entered the state of dream.
I am Prājña, the presiding divine self, the sphere of the substratum of the universe, / established in deep sleep, indifferent to the world, imagined [variously].
I am the fourth (Turīya), changeless, free from the states of the guṇas, / untainted, like a witness, having a form reflected in the universe.
A semblance of consciousness, bliss of consciousness, consisting of consciousness, having the nature of consciousness, / eternal, imperishable, having the form of Brahman: thus know me, O Brahmā."
The Blessed Lord said: / Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu previously concealed his form from Brahmā. / And he too, having understood the pervasion of the universe, became fulfilled in an instant.
O king, you too are purified in soul simply through the birth of Pṛthu; / nevertheless, worship the all-pervading lord with this hymn, O one of good vows.'
Pleased, Viṣṇu said to him: 'Choose a boon, O giver of honor.' / Vena said: 'Grant me a good destination, O Viṣṇu; deliver me from wickedness.
I have come to you for refuge; tell me the cause of a good destination.' / Viṣṇu said: 'Previously indeed, O fortunate one, by the high-souled Aṅga,
I was worshipped by him, and a boon was granted to him by me: / "You will go, O fortunate one, to the supreme realm of Viṣṇu,
by your own action, O chief of brāhmaṇas, by your merit, O son of a king." / For your own sake, O fortunate one, ask for a boon.
Listen, O fortunate Vena, to the account of previous events. / Formerly, a curse was given to your mother, O king, when angered,
by the high-souled Suśaṅkha to Sunīthā in her childhood previously. / Then a boon was granted to Aṅga by me, whose self was known,
desiring to deliver you: "A good son will be born to you." / Having spoken thus to your father, I, affectionate toward virtues,
[thought:] "Arising from your body, I shall protect the world. / As Indra shines in heaven, so I am situated on the surface of the earth.
'The self is indeed born as a son'—thus the Vedic scripture is truthful. / Therefore, my child, you will obtain a good destination from my boon."
For your own higher destination, O king, perform single-minded gifting; / [for] I, who am the form of sin born of Sunīthā, O scorcher of foes,
spoke in naked form to make you depart from dharma. / For otherwise, the very word of Suśaṅkha would become untrue.
Therefore, both injunction and prohibition are indeed myself, O best of kings, / the granter of fruits according to deeds, beyond intellect, seizing all qualities.
Gifting alone is supreme and best; gifting is the effectuator of all. / Therefore, give gifts; from gifting merit proceeds.
By gifting, sin is destroyed; therefore, indeed, give gifts! / Sacrifice with sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice, O best of kings!
Give gifts such as the gift of land to Brahmins. / From proper gifting enjoyment is obtained; from proper gifting renown is attained.
From proper gifting fame arises; from proper gifting happiness is gained. / By gifting one attains heaven, and enjoys the fruit there.
When proper gift is given endowed with faith, O best of men, / when the time arrives, one goes to a sacred ford: this is the fruit of merit.
Whoever gives a great gift to a worthy Brahmin / with a mind purified by faith, fixing his thought upon me,
to him I give everything, whatever he desires in his mind. / Vena said: / Tell me the time for gifting; what is the characteristic of the time?
And what is the nature of a sacred ford, and the good characteristic of a worthy recipient? / O Lord of the world, tell me also the rite of gifting in detail,
showing a gracious countenance, if there is compassion for me. / Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: / I will declare the time for gifting, both regular and occasional, O king,
and the optional, O great king, and the fourth which brings attainment. / At the time of sunrise, sin is destroyed on every side.
Excessive dark terrors bring destruction to men; / the sun in the sky is this portion of mine, established as a treasure-house of lights.
Burnt by his very radiance, sins turn to ashes. / Whoever gives even water, having seen my rising portion,
what can be said of him, O king? His merit increases daily. / When that auspicious time has arrived, a man performing meritorious acts,
having bathed and worshipped the ancestors and gods, should become a giver of gifts / according to his capacity and power, with a mind purified by faith:
food, milk, fruit, flowers, cloth, betel, ornaments, / and gold, gems, and the like; his merit is infinite.
Then at midday, O king, and likewise in the afternoon, / whoever gives with reference to me, his merit is infinite:
food, drink, sweet ointment, fragrant paste, saffron, / and camphor and the like, together with cloth and ornaments.
He who thus gives uninterruptedly, bestowing the happiness of enjoyment— / this regular time has been declared by me as auspicious for those who seek [the fruit of] gifts and worship.
Now next I shall declare the occasional, which is unexcelled. / Even at the three divisions of the day, a gift must certainly be given, without doubt.
One who desires his own welfare must not make a day empty [of gifts]. / At whatever time some gift is given, O ruler of men,
by that power he becomes very wise, endowed with great capability, / wealthy, virtuous, sagacious, learned, and discerning.
When food has not been given for a fortnight, a month, or a day, / I ward off that very best of men from food.
His own impurity is eaten by not giving an excellent gift. / I produce disease, which wards off all enjoyment,
in their bodies when I am displeased, causing much affliction, / accompanied by sluggish digestive fire, causing the burning heat of fever.
By those who have not given at the three divisions of the day to Brahmins and gods, / but eat sweets themselves, a great sin has been committed.
One should purify such a person by means of severe expiation, / by fasts that emaciate the body and so forth, O great king.
Just as a leatherworker, merciless over a hide resting in a pit, / cleanses it with astringent decoctions and softens that hide,
so do I cleanse the doer of sin, without a doubt, / through the proper application of medicines, and surely with bitter astringents,
with hot water, and through torments in the form of a physician, not otherwise. / Others enjoy his terrible, meritorious pleasures that follow the mind.
Though capable, what does he do when an excellent gift has not been given? / In the form of great sin, I torment him thus.
When the gift belonging to the regular time has not been given by sinners for their own sake / with a mind purified by faith, O king of kings,
then I consume them by means of dreadful expedients indeed. / Vāsudeva said: / I will also declare the occasional time and its merit before you,
O best of men; listen attentively with a good intellect: / the new moon day, O great king, and likewise the full moon day,
when a solstice or equinox occurs, the Vyatīpāta yoga, O lord of men, / and when Vaidhṛti is declared, and when the eleventh lunar day occurs,
the great full moon of Māgha, and that of Āṣāḍha, of Vaiśākha, and of Kārttika, / on the conjunction of the new moon and Monday, on the beginnings of Manvantaras and the beginnings of Yugas,
the Gajacchāyā conjunction as declared, and likewise the Pitṛkṣaya day— / these occasional times are declared before you, O best of kings.
A gift is given on these occasions; whatever fruit belongs to that gift, / that fruit I shall declare; let it be heard, O best of kings.
When a man gives with devotion to a Brahmin, dedicating it to me, / I give to him without hesitation, without a doubt,
a house, happiness, O great king, heaven, liberation, and much else. / I shall declare the optional time, which yields the fruits of gifting:
for all vows indeed, and likewise for deities and so forth; / the meritorious time for gifting has been proclaimed by the best of twice-borns.
I shall also declare to you the time relating to prosperity, O king: / on all sacrifices, on the unexcelled marriage ceremony,
as soon as a son is born, at the tonsure, investiture with the sacred grass-girdle, and so forth, / on the consecration and other rites of temples, flagstaffs, and deities,
on reservoirs, wells, and ponds, and concerning house-construction, O king— / that is declared the time relating to prosperity, wherein there is worship of the Mothers.
At that time one should give a gift that grants all accomplishments; / this very time is called the time relating to prosperity, O best of kings.
And I will declare another, which averts the affliction of sin: / when the time of death has arrived, knowing the body's end, O best of men,
a gift should be given then, which bestows happiness on Yama's path. / The regular and occasional times, and likewise the optional and prosperity-related,
and the final time, O great king, have been declared before you; / these times have been proclaimed, granting the fruits of one's own deeds.
I shall declare the characteristic of a sacred ford before you, O king: / among good sacred fords, this Gaṅgā shines, and the holy Sarasvatī,
the Revā, the Yamunā, the Tāpī, and the river Carmaṇvatī, / the Sarayū, the Ghargharā, the Veṇā, destroying all sins,
the Kāverī, the Kapilā, and another, the Viśālā that carries all across, / the Godāvarī so called, and the Tuṅgabhadrā, O best of men,
the Bhīmarathī, proclaimed as ever terrifying to sins, / the Devikā, the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā, and other supreme and excellent rivers.
At meritorious times, there are many sacred fords along these; / whether in a village or in a forest, rivers are purifying everywhere.
Rites such as bathing and giving gifts should be performed in each of them / when their names and that of the sacred place are not known, O best of men.
One should pronounce the name: “This is Viṣṇu’s sacred place,” O king. / The deity of that sacred place is likewise myself, without doubt.
The practitioner who thus mentions me at a sacred place among the gods, / the meritorious fruit of that comes through my name, O son of the king.
At unknown holy places and deities, O best of kings, / during bathing and giving gifts, O great king, one should indeed pronounce my name.
O lord of kings, these sacred places were created by the Creator for the earth; / they are oceans of all merits, situated everywhere on the terrestrial sphere.
Wherever they are, bathing and giving gifts should be performed, O king; / one obtains imperishable fruit by the grace of the holy places.
The seven oceans are themselves sacred places of great merit, / and the lakes beginning with Mānasa are likewise celebrated, O king.
Cascades and ponds are said to be forms of sacred places, without doubt. / In small rivers too, O great king, a sacred place is established.
And likewise in all excavated pools, with the exception of an ordinary well. / Mountains too are forms of sacred places, such as Meru and others on earth.
The ground of sacrifice, the sacrifice itself, and as situated in the agnihotra; / the ground for ancestral rites when pure, and again the hall of the gods;
the hall of oblations likewise, and the house where the Veda is studied; / in homes, an excellent cowshed endowed with merit;
wherever a drinker of Soma may be, there a sacred place is established; / where there is a meritorious grove, and where an aśvattha tree stands;
where there is a Brahmā-tree, and likewise a banyan tree, / and others in a forested place—there a sacred place is established.
These are declared to be sacred places, and likewise a father and a mother; / where the Purāṇa is recited, and where the guru himself resides;
where a virtuous wife stays, there is a sacred place without doubt; / where a good son stays, there is a sacred place without doubt.
These are declared to be sacred places, and likewise a royal palace. / Vena said: / Tell me the marks of an eligible recipient to whom gifts should be given, O best of gods,
turning your face favorably in grace toward me, O Mādhava. / Vāsudeva said: / Listen, O king of great wisdom, to the auspicious marks of an eligible recipient
to whom a good gift is to be given by great-souled persons purified by faith: / a brāhmaṇa endowed with a noble lineage, devoted to the study of the Veda,
tranquil, self-controlled, endowed with austerity, especially of pure conduct, / prudent, wise, devoted to worshiping the gods,
truthful, exceedingly meritorious, a Vaiṣṇava, learned in knowledge, / knowing dharma, freed from fickleness, and free from heretics.
Such an eligible recipient has been declared; I shall mention another in the same way: / a sister's son endowed with these virtues, O best among men—
know him to be an eligible recipient; then a daughter's son, / and a son-in-law, O great king, endowed with these qualities;
and the guru and an initiated person are deemed eligible recipients, O best of men. / These alone are suitable recipients worthy of gifts, O best of men.
Even if endowed with Vedic conduct, one who never attains contentment— / one should certainly avoid that priest, as well as one who is one-eyed and very deceitful.
One should avoid a person who is extremely dark, O great king, or tawny, / one with crab-like eyes, one who is deep blue-black, and one with dark teeth.
Likewise, O king, one with blue teeth, and also one with yellow teeth, / a cow-killer, one with black teeth, a barbarian, and one covered in dust,
one with a deficient limb or an extra limb, a leper, one with deformed nails, / one with diseased skin, O great king, and a bald man—one should avoid them.
A priest whose wife is engaged in misconduct— / a gift should not be given to him, even if he were equal to Brahmā.
A gift should not be given to a henpecked man, nor to a debauchee, O intelligent one, / nor to a diseased person, nor to those who eat offerings for the dead, O lord of earth.
And a gift should not be given to a thief, even if he were equal to Atri; / it should not be given to an insatiable man, and one should avoid one under funeral pollution.
It should not be given to one who is exceedingly stubborn, and especially not to a rogue. / One endowed with the Vedas and śāstras but devoid of good conduct
should never be employed in ancestral rites or gifts, O lord of kings. / Now I shall declare the gift that is fruitful and yields merit.

Through the presence of faith, the right time, holy place, and suitable recipients are fulfilled. / There is no merit equal to faith; there is no happiness equal to faith.

There is no sacred place equal to faith for living beings in this cycle of existence, O king. / Endowed with an attitude of faith, one should remember me thus.
A gift should be placed into the hand of an eligible recipient, even if small, O best of kings. / The fruit that comes from such a gift performed according to the rules,
one attains that endlessly, and becomes happy through my grace.

2.40.m: Vena said: / The fruit of constant gifts has previously been heard by me from you, O deity. / As for the fruit of an occasional gift when given,
explain that fruit to me carefully through your grace; / I do not feel fully satisfied, and faith to hear arises.
Viṣṇu said: / I shall declare the occasional gift, O best of kings. / When a great festival has arrived, by whom gifts are given with faith
to worthy recipients, hear the meritorious fruit of that! / He who gives an elephant, a chariot, or even a horse, O best of kings,
accompanied by servants, becomes a superior king in a holy land; / indeed, he is born, O great king, through my grace, without doubt.
He becomes a righteous king, knowledgeable, powerful, and intelligent; / unconquerable by all beings, he is born endowed with great splendor.
When a great festival has arrived, whoever makes a gift of land / or a gift of a cow, O great king, becomes a master of all enjoyments.
One should diligently make a gift to a highly meritorious brāhmaṇa. / He who gives the great gifts at a sacred place on an auspicious festival, knowing the recipient—
I shall declare their distinguishing mark: kingship arises [for him]. / When an auspicious festival has arrived at a sacred place, he who makes a secret gift,
swift attainment of treasures, imperishable, comes about. / When a great festival has arrived at sacred places, and to a brāhmaṇa
a great gift of fine cloth endowed with gold [is made], / I shall declare the meritorious fruit of that gift, O lord of earth.
Many virtuous sons are born, masters of the Vedas, / long-lived, rich in offspring, and endowed with fame and merit.
Abundant and prosperous fortune is born, O wise one; / he obtains pure happiness and becomes righteous.
When a great festival has arrived, having gone diligently to a sacred place, / one should give a brown cow adorned with gold to a great-souled brāhmaṇa.
I shall declare the merit of that gift, O wise one: / the giver of a brown cow, O great king, enjoys all pleasures;
he remains there as long as Brahmā lives. / When a great festival has arrived, then having decorated a cow
furnished with gold, and with garments and ornaments— / I shall describe the enjoyment of the fruit of that gift, O lord of kings:
abundant fortune arises, filled with giving and enjoyment; / having become master of all branches of learning, he indeed becomes devoted to Viṣṇu.
A mortal dwells in Viṣṇu's world as long as the earth stands, / but whoever goes to a holy ford and gives an ornament to a brāhmaṇa,
