having enjoyed vast pleasures, sports together with Indra. / When a great festival arrives, [giving] clothing to a bull among the twice-born,
and having given food together with land in a vessel, accompanied by faith, / he rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha, his prowess equal to Viṣṇu's.
Having given gold together with clothing to a twice-born for his satisfaction, / he dwells happily in Vaikuṇṭha at his own pleasure, resembling fire.
One should fill a fine pitcher of gold with ghee; / a silver lid should be made, adorned with garments and necklaces.
One should endow it with garlands of flowers and adorn it with a sacred thread. / Consecrated with Vedic mantras, having worshipped it, O highly wise one,
one should worship it with the sixteen pure offerings. / Having decorated it well, one should then give it to a great-souled brāhmaṇa.
Then sixteen cows clothed in garments, with bronze milking-pails, / and four endowed with pitchers, and a sacrificial fee with gold;
likewise, twelve cows adorned with garments and ornaments / should be given separately to a vipra; of this there is no doubt.
Beginning with these, other gifts, O joy of kings, / upon properly reaching a pilgrimage time or the dwelling of a vipra,
should be given with a spirit of faith; it produces abundant merit. / Viṣṇu said: / Whatever gift is made intending Viṣṇu, conceived with a desire,
permeated with intention through the spirit of that gift, / a human being enjoys a corresponding fruit; of this there is no doubt.
I shall declare the prosperity that arises in sacrifices and the like; / by that gift of his, and through faith, O best of the twice-born,
he attains an increase of wisdom and meets with no sorrow. / The righteous person enjoys pleasures while yet alive now.
Having attained a divine state, that giver enjoys the pleasures of Indra; / he leads his own family to heaven for a thousand kalpas.
Thus the prosperity obtained among them has been declared; I shall speak [further]: / having known the wasting of the body, afflicted by old age,
he should make a gift; he should not place hope in anyone: / ‘And when I am dead, my sons and other kin and relatives,
how will these friends of mine fare without me?’ / Bewildered through delusion concerning them, he gives nothing at all.
His mind deluded, he goes to death; his friends and relatives weep, / all afflicted by grief, afflicted by the delusion of māyā.
They promise gifts and contemplate liberation; / but when he is dead, O great king, and the delusion of māyā has passed,
they forget the gifts; greedy-minded, they do not give. / That man who has died, O great king, exceedingly miserable on Yama's path,
overcome by thirst and hunger, tormented by many sorrows— / therefore a gift should be given by oneself alone; of this there is no doubt.
Whose sons and grandsons? Whose wife, O best of kings? / In saṃsāra no one belongs to anyone; therefore a gift is given.
By one who possesses knowledge it should be given by oneself alone, no doubt: / food, drink, betel, water, and likewise gold,
a pair of garments, and an umbrella, by oneself alone, no doubt; / many water-vessels filled with water, O best of kings,
variegated vehicles and conveyances, O highly wise one, / various fragrances with camphor—which bestow comfort on Yama's path.
Sandals should be given if one desires abundant ease. / By these gifts, O great king, upon Yama's path happily indeed
a mortal travels, O king, adorned by Yama's messengers.

2.41.m: Vena said: / Tell how a son is a holy ford, how a wife, how a father and mother; / and how a teacher is a holy ford—tell me that in detail.
The auspicious Viṣṇu said: / There is a charming great city, Vārāṇasī, joined with the Gaṅgā. / In it lives a vaiśya, Kṛkala by name.
His wife is deeply virtuous, dedicated to her husband as a vow, / ever devoted to the practice of dharma, devoted solely to her husband,
Sutalā by name, of meritorious body, with fine sons, lovely and auspicious, / speaking truth, ever pure, lovely in form, dear to her beloved.
Endowed with such virtues, fortunate, acting beautifully. / That excellent vaiśya was knowledgeable in various dharmas, wise, and virtuous,
ever intent on hearing the Purāṇa and the Vedic dharma. / In connection with a pilgrimage to holy fords, which grants abundant merit,
he set out with faith on the pilgrimage to holy fords, meritorious and auspicious, / in the company of brāhmaṇas and with that caravan leader.
As he set forth on the path of dharma, the devoted wife spoke to him; / infatuated with love for her husband, she said these words to her husband:
Sukalā said: / According to dharma I am your wife, performing merit together [with you], my beloved. / Waiting upon the way of my husband, I worship my husband as a god.
At no time should nearness to you be abandoned by me, O best of the twice-born. / Taking shelter in your shadow, I shall perform the highest dharma,
known as fidelity to one's husband, which destroys sin and grants a destination to women. / A woman is called virtuous in the world who is devoted to her husband.
For young women, a separate holy ford without a husband does not look well; / it does not bring comfort in the world, nor does it bestow heaven and liberation.
Know the right foot of a husband to be Prayāga, O best of men, / and the woman who considers his left [foot] to be Puṣkara—
from bathing in the water of his feet, that merit is generated; / bathing [there] is equal to Prayāga and Puṣkara for women, no doubt.
A husband consists of all holy fords; a husband consists of all merits. / The merit that belongs to an initiate from the offering of sacrifices,
that fruit one certainly obtains solely through service to the husband. / Whatever arises from making a pilgrimage to holy fords such as Gayā,
that fruit one obtains even from attending upon the husband. / I shall explain it concisely; hear that from me as I speak:
For them there is indeed no separate dharma without attendance on the husband. / Therefore, my beloved, acting as your companion, giving comfort,
taking shelter in your shadow, I shall come; not otherwise. / Viṣṇu said: / Observing her beauty, character, virtue, devotion, and also her youth,
and reflecting thus again and again on her delicate nature, that Kṛkala [thought]: / ‘If indeed I lead her along a difficult and very painful path,
the destruction of her beauty would occur from the agitation of cold and heat. / Her bodily complexion resembles the interior of a lotus;
by stormy wind and cold it will become dark-colored. / The path is rough with sharp stones, and her two feet are very tender;
she will encounter sharp pain, and then be unable to walk. / Her limbs overcome by hunger and thirst, what will she become?
She of lovely face is my left side and my place of comfort, / ever dearer to me than life, and ever the support of dharma.
If this young woman meets destruction, my destruction would occur here. / She is my constant livelihood; she is the mistress of my life.
I will not lead her to the forest and the holy ford, and I alone shall go.’ / Having thought for a moment indeed, by the great-souled Kṛkala,
His inner intention was understood by her, O best of kings. / Then the illustrious lady spoke again to her husband as he was setting out:
“Listen, O best [of men]! A sinless [wife] must never be abandoned by men. / For she is the very root of dharma for a man, O highly intelligent one!
Knowing this, O fortunate one, take me with you now!” / Viṣṇu said: Having heard everything, even the many things said with good intentions by his beloved,
Kṛkala, laughing, spoke this word to her again: / “A wife acquired in accordance with dharma, O dear one, must never be abandoned.
By him who has abandoned a well-behaved wife who practices dharma, / the ten-limbed dharma has also been abandoned, O fair-faced one.
Therefore, blessings be upon you, I will never abandon you, O beloved!” / Viṣṇu said: Having thus spoken to his wife and consoled her again and again,
he departed with a caravan without her knowledge. / When that illustrious Kṛkala of meritorious deeds had gone,
at the time of divine rituals, at the auspicious hour, the fair-faced lady / did not see her husband Kṛkala in their house.
Rising up in haste, weeping and extremely miserable, / stricken by the agony of sorrow and grief, she asked her husband’s companions:
“Have you seen that Kṛkala of mine, O noble ones? / The lord of my life has gone somewhere; you are my kinsmen.
If you have seen my Kṛkala now, O noble ones, / my husband, the doer of meritorious deeds, all-knowing, wise in truth,
tell me of that great soul, if the wise one has been seen.” / Hearing those words of hers, they said to that wise woman:
“Your lord Kṛkala, O auspicious lady, in connection with a religious journey, / has undertaken a pilgrimage to holy fords. Why do you grieve, O woman of virtuous vows?
Having accomplished [his visit to] the great holy ford, he will return, O lovely one!” / Having been thus consoled by those trustworthy men,
Sukalā, charming of speech, went back home, O king. / Sukalā, devoted [to her lord], wept piteously in sorrow:
“Until my husband returns, I will sleep on a straw pallet on the ground. / I will not eat ghee or oil, nor curds or milk.
Salt is abandoned, as well as betel-leaf. / Sweet food also, O king, such as jaggery and the like, is given up.
Taking one meal a day or fasting altogether, I shall remain thus, without a doubt, / until the return of my husband comes to pass once more.”
Becoming thus stricken with grief, wearing a single braid, / clad in a single bodice, she became soiled.
Clad in a single dirty garment, she remained, / uttering cries of lamentation, sighing, intensely grieved,
burned by the fire of separation, her limbs darkened, wearing dirt. / Thus full of sorrowful conduct, she was very emaciated and bewildered then.
Weeping day and night, she obtained no sleep at night; / shattered by grief, she felt no hunger, O king.
Then her female friends arrived and asked Sukalā: / “O Sukalā of charming limbs, why do you weep now?
Tell us the cause of this grief, O fair-faced one!” / Sukalā said: “Abandoning me, my husband, devoted to dharma, has gone for the sake of dharma.
On the occasion of a pilgrimage to holy fords, he wanders the earth from here. / Leaving me, faultless and free from sin, the master has departed.
I am of virtuous conduct, ever pure, a devoted wife. / Abandoning me, my husband has gone, intent on attaining [the merit of] holy fords.
Because of that I am grieving, O friends, greatly tormented by separation. / The destruction of life is better; far better is the eating of poison;
entering the fire is better; the destruction of the body is better! / Abandoning his beloved woman, the husband has gone, utterly cruel.
Separation from the husband is not preferable; the surrender of life is better, O friend! / I am not able to endure this ever-dreadful separation.
Because of that I am constantly grieving from separation, O friends!” / The friends said: “Your husband has gone on a pilgrimage to holy fords; your lord will return.
In vain do you wither your body; in vain do you grieve indeed! / In vain do you torment yourself, young woman; in vain do you abandon pleasures!
Drink your drink, enjoy what was previously given to you by yourself! / Whose is a husband? Whose are sons? Whose are kinsmen and relatives?
Who belongs to whom in worldly existence? There is truly no connection with anyone. / What is eaten and enjoyed, O young woman, that alone is the fruit of worldly existence.
When a living being is dead, who eats? Who indeed sees that fruit? / What is drunk and enjoyed, O young woman, this is the fruit of worldly existence.”
Sukalā said: “What you have said cannot be approved by the Veda. / The woman who, separated from her husband, lives always alone,
becomes a sinful woman; virtuous people do not respect her. / Along with the husband, O friends, is seen always in the Vedas;
the connection arises from association with merit, there is no doubt about this. / And the husband is always proclaimed in the treatises to be the holy ford for women.
One should ever invoke him alone by speech, body, and actions; / one should ever worship him in mind, intent on truth of feeling.
The husband’s side—his right limb—is always a great holy ford. / Relying on that, when a housewife conducts herself,
and sacrifices with the merits of giving, whatever fruit comes from that giving, / whatever fruit is at Vārāṇasī, at the Gaṅgā, and not at Puṣkara,
nor at Dvārakā, nor at Avantī, nor at Kedāra of the moon-adorned [Śiva], / that woman, always sacrificing, indeed does not obtain
such fruit ever, O friend! / A pleasant face, good fortune with sons, bathing, gifting, ornaments,
clothing, ornaments, good fortune, beauty, radiance, constant fruit, / fame, renown, and virtue—the fair-complexioned woman attains [them all].
From the husband's favor she obtains everything, there is no doubt about this. / When the beloved is present, if she performs any other religious duty,
it becomes fruitless for her; she is declared an unchaste woman. / The youth and beauty of women is remembered as a descent [of grace] indeed
for the sake of the one husband alone upon the earthly sphere. / A woman having good sons and renowned is always declared [as such].
When the husband is pleased, a woman is worthy to be beheld in the world, without doubt. / If a woman is bereft of her husband on the earthly realm,
whence comes her happiness, beauty, fame, renown, or sons on earth? / Utter misfortune and great sorrow are experienced in worldly existence.
She becomes a sharer in sin, of mournful conduct at all times. / But when her husband is pleased, all the deities are pleased.
When the husband is pleased, the sages, gods, and mortals are pleased. / The husband is the master, the husband is the guru, the husband is the deity along with the deities.
The husband is the holy ford and the merit for women, O son of the king. / Adornment, ornaments, beauty, complexion, and fragrant scent—
having applied them, she should ever remain, except on auspicious festival days. / She shone with adornments and ornaments when her husband was present.
Without the husband, it is just like milk in the mouth of a serpent. / For the sake of the husband, an illustrious woman observes good vows and brings charming blessings.
When the husband is away, if a woman adorns herself, / all that beauty and complexion becomes like that of a corpse.
People on earth say, ‘She is an unchaste woman, no doubt.’ / Therefore, hear, [how it is] on earth for a woman separated from her husband:
desiring great happiness, [a wife] must always behave [virtually]; / the husband is sung in the scriptures as the supreme duty of a good wife.
Therefore, eternal duty should never be abandoned by a wife. / Knowing such dharma, how could a husband abandon [her]?
In this regard, O friend, an ancient legendary history is heard, / along with the very holy, sin-destroying conduct of Sudevā.

2.42.m: The friends said: / Who was Sudevā mentioned by you? What was her conduct? Tell us! / You have mentioned her, O fortunate one; tell us the very truth!
Sukalā said: / In Ayodhyā there was a great king, skilled in dharma, / the son of Manu, highly fortunate, intent upon all dharma and wealth,
named Ikṣvāku, omniscient, a worshiper of gods and Brahmins. / His wife was always virtuous and devoted to her husband.
With her he would perform sacrifices and visit various holy places. / Of the heroic Vedarāja, the high-souled lord of Kāśī,
there was a daughter named Sudevā, devoted to righteous conduct. / The great king Ikṣvāku, ruler of the earth, married her.
Sudevā was beautiful in all her limbs, devoted to the vow of truth. / Together with her, that king, the holy leader of the people,
that tiger among kings, always delighted with that beloved [queen]. / But once the great king went with her to the forest.
Reaching the forest of the Gaṅgā, he continually engaged in hunting, / killing lions, boars, elephants, and buffaloes.
While he was thus sporting, a boar came before him, / accompanied by a large herd of swine, surrounded by sons and grandsons.
And one sow, his beloved, stood by his side; / she was encircled by the boars and swine around him.
And seeing the supreme king of kings, invincible, intent upon the hunt, / taking refuge at the base of a mountain together with his wife, the boar,
stood alone, by great valor, [protecting] his sons, grandsons, elders, and young ones, / knowing the great slaughter of those beasts by the king.
That boar said to those sons, grandsons, and wife: / "The heroic lord of Kośala, the son of Manu, endowed with great strength,
is sporting in the hunt, O beloved, and is slaying many beasts. / Seeing me, the great king will certainly come here, without doubt.
From other hunters, truly, I have no fear for my life; / but seeing my form, the king will never show mercy.
Filled with great joy, holding arrows in hand and bearing a bow, / accompanied by dogs, endowed with great splendor, surrounded by hunters,
O beloved, he will surely kill me; of this there is no doubt."
The sow said: / "Whenever you see many hunters equipped with weapons in the great forest, O beloved, / together with these sons and my grandsons, you would flee far away.

Abandoning great steadfastness, power, and high manhood, your mind despondent with great fear, / what are you doing now upon seeing the lord of kings, the best of the best of men? Tell the reason, O beloved!"
Hearing her words, the boar, king of swine, spoke this reply to her: / "The reason I feared ordinary hunters, O beloved, and seeing them went far away after warning the swine—
evil hunters are wicked sinners, O beloved; they commit sins in mountain strongholds and caves; / always wicked, intent on many sins, they are all born into a family of absolute sinners.
Indeed, I fear death at their hands; even when dead, I would incur sin again; / fearing an untimely death, O beloved, I would flee far away to a mountain and a mountain cave.

But this righteous lord of men who has arrived is superior to all the world, a king who is the very form of Keśava. / I will wage battle in combat with this high-souled one, O beloved, with manly valor.
If I conquer the king by my own splendor, I will enjoy unequaled fame on earth; / struck down by him, the best of heroes, in battle, I will go to the world of Madhusūdana.

By the meat and fat of my body, the lord of the earth will attain supreme satisfaction; / the deities of the fair realms will be pleased, and from this, he, the wielder of the thunderbolt, has arrived.

When death comes to me at his very hand, my gain will be the highest glory, O beautiful one; / therefore, with renown upon the surface of the earth in the three worlds, I will go to the realm of Madhusūdana.
It is not that I fled to the mountain peaks because I was frightened or agitated; / I fled out of fear of sin, O beloved, but seeing dharma, I now stand firm.
I do not know what sin was accumulated by me previously in another birth, / because of which accumulation of sin I entered the womb of a boar.
I will wash away that terrible accumulation of prior sin / with the waters of arrows, exceedingly terrible, extremely sharp, honed in their hundreds.
Taking the sons, grandsons, daughters, and young family, O sow, / go to the mountain, and cast off this delusion concerning me.
Renounce your affection for me; this Hari has arrived. / From his hand, I shall go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Today indeed, by destiny, the unsurpassed gate of heaven / has its doors thrown open for me; I shall go to the great heaven."
Sukalā said: / Hearing those words of that high-souled boar, / his beloved then spoke to him, her inner soul distressed, O friends.
The sow said: / "In the herd where you are the master, adorned with sons and grandsons, / with friends and brothers, and with other kinsmen and relatives,
adorned solely by you, the herd shines because of you; / without you, O fortunate one, what kind of herd will it become?
Only by your own strength, roaring, do the boars / and my young sons roam upon the mountain, O beloved.
Fearless by your splendor, they eat good bulbs and roots / in strongholds, forest thickets, villages, and towns.
They do not feel intense fear of lions here on the mountain, / nor of men, O mighty-armed one, protected as they are by your splendor.
Abandoned by you, all these young children of mine / will become miserable, bewildered, and unconscious.
Continually the young ones look, having gone on a pleasant path; / just as a woman bereft of her husband, though lovely, does not shine at all,
even if adorned with celestial ornaments together with gold, / with possessions, jewels, and garments, and accompanied by father, mother, and brothers,
mother-in-law, father-in-law, and others, bereft of her husband she does not shine, / just as a night without the moon, or a family without a son,
or a house without a lamp never shines at all; / even so, without you, this herd will not shine, O giver of honor.
Just as a mortal without proper conduct, an ascetic without knowledge, / or a king without counsel does not shine, so this [herd] will not shine.
Just as a boat full [of cargo] in the ocean does not shine without a helmsman, / and just as a caravan does not shine without a caravan-leader,
and just as an army does not shine without a commander, / so indeed this army of boars without you, O wise one,
will become miserable, like a Brahmin devoid of the Veda. / Placing the burden of the family upon me, you are departing!
Knowing death to be easy, what kind of resolve is this of yours? / Without you, I am unable to maintain my life, O beloved lord!"
Only together with you shall I experience heaven, or earth, O highly intelligent one, / or even hell; truly, truly do I say this.
Either you, taking our sons and grandsons, the excellent herd, / let us both go, O leader of the herd, to an impassable, fine cave like that.
Abandoning life, one goes forth to battle; / what gain is seen in dying there? Speak now.
The boar said: / "You do not know the highest duty of heroes; hear it now. / When a hero who desires battle goes and begs of [another] hero:
'Grant me a fight in battle! Desiring combat, I have come!' / when a man does not grant the battle begged for by an adversary,
out of desire, greed, fear, or delusion—hear, O beloved— / he dwells in the Kumbhīpāka hell for a thousand yugas.
For Kṣatriyas, this is the supreme duty: battle must be granted, no doubt. / When that battle is granted by one who has gone to the battlefield,
and the enemy is conquered there, they enjoy fame and renown. / Or, fighting utterly fearlessly with manly courage, he is slain;
he attains the realm of heroes and enjoys celestial pleasures. / Hear, beloved: for twenty-one thousand years
he dwells in the realm of heroes and is honored with divine conduct. / This son of Manu has arrived, a hero without doubt.
Since he begs for battle, combat must certainly be granted by me. / A guest for battle has arrived, an eternal form of Viṣṇu;

and hospitality must be offered by me in the form of battle, O auspicious one."
The sow said: / "Since battle must be granted by you to the great-souled king,

then, my love, I shall see what your manly courage is like."
Having spoken thus, quickly summoning her dear sons,
she said: "O sons, listen to my words! / A guest for battle has arrived, an eternal form of Viṣṇu.
I must go to where this one will go. / As long as the protector, your lord, stands,
go far away to the mouth of an impassable mountain cave. / Live happily, my children, avoiding the greedy hunters.
I must go only where this one will go. / This eldest brother of yours will protect the herd.
All these uncles are your protectors. / Go far away, all of you, leaving me behind, my good sons."
The sons said: / "Indeed, this excellent mountain has abundant roots, fruits, and water. / None of us has any fear; indeed, our life is happy.
Why has this dreadful thing been spoken all at once by both of you? / Therefore, O mother, tell us truly right here the reason for it."
The sow said: / "This king has arrived, very ferocious, the very form of Death. / Passionate for hunting, he sports, having slain many deer in the forest.
His name is Ikṣvāku, invincible, the mighty son of Manu. / This Death will destroy [us]; go far away, good sons!"
The sons said: / "That evil-minded one who goes away abandoning mother and father / goes to a very terrifying, dreadful hell.
Having drunk his mother's holy milk, does he become ruthless? / That very weak-minded one who goes away abandoning mother and father
goes here to a hell of pus, filled with worms and foul smells. / Therefore, leaving our mother and elder behind, we shall not go from here."
Thus their sorrow arose, united with righteousness and purpose. / Forming a battle array, they all stood, full of strength and splendor.
Endowed with daring and vigor, they looked upon the prince, / roaring, endowed with manly courage, sporting in the forest then.
